part_title: KMS Envelope Encryption, Key Ownership, Snapshots and Macie

scenes.title: AWS KMS envelope encryption
scenes.narration: Follow the encrypt path in the upper half. The application requests a data key from AWS KMS. KMS returns a plaintext data key for immediate encryption together with an encrypted version protected by a KMS key. The application uses the plaintext key locally to encrypt the file, then stores the encrypted file beside its encrypted data key. The long-term master key remains protected by KMS; the application doesn't use it to encrypt every byte of a large object. Now follow the decrypt path. Retrieve the encrypted data key, ask KMS to decrypt that key under the appropriate permissions, then use the recovered plaintext data key to decrypt the file. The security advantage is separation between bulk data encryption and key management, with fine-grained use permissions and auditability. The lower IAM example grants GenerateDataKey and Decrypt rather than powerful key-administration operations such as disabling a KMS key or scheduling deletion. Treat the plaintext data key as sensitive, keep it only as long as needed and avoid logging it. Envelope encryption scales without giving each application permission to manage the KMS key itself.

scenes.title: KMS key types and ownership
scenes.narration: This comparison has three columns, each representing a different level of key control. AWS-owned keys are operated by AWS for internal service encryption and aren't directly administered by customers. AWS-managed KMS keys are created in your account on behalf of a service, often shown with aliases like aws slash s3 or aws slash ebs. Their lifecycle and policy customisation are limited. Customer-managed KMS keys are created and controlled by you, with configurable key policies, access grants and rotation choices where supported. Follow the rotation, policy and typical-use rows rather than judging only by the names. A workload that simply needs default encryption can often use a managed option. Cross-account sharing, explicit separation of duties and particular compliance controls may call for customer-managed keys. A customer-managed key introduces operating responsibilities too: permissions, monitoring, rotation planning and recovery from accidental disabling. Key rotation behavior and pricing depend on key type and current KMS capabilities, so avoid treating the slide's example intervals as universal. Choose the least complex key ownership model that meets the data-control requirement.

scenes.title: Cross-Region Encrypted Snapshot Copy
scenes.narration: The diagram begins with an encrypted snapshot in one AWS Region and follows a copy request to a second Region. The source snapshot remains protected under its source KMS key. During the copy, AWS accesses the encrypted snapshot subject to permissions and creates a new encrypted copy using a KMS key in the destination Region. The arrows show a secure transfer and a separate destination encryption boundary; merely copying a source key identifier across Regions is not sufficient. Look at the permission panels below. The request needs permission to perform the snapshot copy and appropriate access to use the relevant KMS keys, including any required grants. The actual actions and policy requirements depend on the snapshot service, whether the keys are customer managed and whether accounts differ. The benefits panel explains disaster recovery: a regional copy offers geographic separation while maintaining encryption. But a snapshot isn't a complete recovery strategy until you've tested restoration, network connectivity and application dependencies in the destination. Confirm the destination key exists and can be used by the recovery role before relying on the copied backup.

scenes.title: Amazon Macie: Sensitive Data Discovery
scenes.narration: This architecture moves from storage into data discovery. Start with the S3 buckets containing documents, logs or customer records. Amazon Macie uses supported detection methods, including managed data identifiers and pattern-based matching, to identify sensitive information in objects. The findings on the right classify categories such as personal identifiers, credentials and financial data, with a severity and affected object location for investigation. The example finding points to a customer-records PDF and a detected payment-card pattern. Macie reports evidence of possible sensitive data; it does not automatically delete every matching object or decide the correct legal classification for your business. The security team must review the finding, assess whether the object should have been stored there and choose remediation such as limiting bucket access, removing exposed copies or changing ingestion controls. In a GenAI retrieval pipeline, this check is useful before documents are indexed and made available to a model. Review scan scope, permissions and costs, and remember that sensitive data discovery is a complement to encryption and access control rather than a replacement.

scenes.title: Secrets Manager lifecycle
scenes.narration: Read the Secrets Manager lifecycle from left to right. An administrator or authorised automation creates a secret, for example a database credential or external API token. Secrets Manager encrypts the stored value using supported KMS key protection. At runtime, an application using an IAM role requests the secret through GetSecretValue over TLS, so the credential does not need to be committed to source code. The next stage rotates the secret when a supported rotation process is configured, updating the target system and the stored value in coordination. Finally, CloudTrail and relevant operational logging provide evidence of API activity, rotation changes and failures. Notice the lower comparison: credentials hard-coded into a repository can remain in its history, while plain environment variables may be exposed through debugging or overly broad process access. A managed secret doesn't make permissions irrelevant; restrict which identities can read and rotate it, and avoid writing returned values into logs. Rotation also isn't automatic for every secret type without implementation. For a GenAI service integrating external tools, secret lifecycle management should be planned before production.
